prompt: State the two conditions on the resultant force for a body to undergo simple harmonic motion.
markscheme: The force (and so acceleration) is proportional to the displacement from the equilibrium position **(A1)**, and is always directed towards the equilibrium position — opposite to the displacement **(A1)**

prompt: Which graph of acceleration $a$ against displacement $x$ shows simple harmonic motion?
options: A straight line through the origin with positive gradient
A straight line through the origin with negative gradient
markscheme: **B.** $a=-\omega^{2}x$ is a straight line through the origin with negative gradient $-\omega^{2}$. A positive gradient would push the body away from equilibrium.

prompt: A particle oscillates between $x=-4.0$ cm and $x=+4.0$ cm, completing 10 oscillations in 4.0 s. State its amplitude, period and frequency.
markscheme: Amplitude $=4.0$ cm (maximum displacement from equilibrium, not the full 8.0 cm swing) **(A1)**; $T=0.40$ s, $f=2.5$ Hz **(A1)**

prompt: An oscillator has frequency 2.5 Hz. What is its angular frequency?

A 0.40 kg mass oscillates on a spring of spring constant $160\ \text{N m}^{-1}$.

**(a)** Calculate the period. **[2]**

**(b)** State the period if the mass is replaced by a 1.6 kg mass, with a reason. **[1]**
markscheme:
**(a)** $T=2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac mk}=2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{0.40}{160}}=0.31$ s **(M1)(A1)**

**(b)** $T\propto\sqrt m$; four times the mass doubles the period: 0.63 s **(A1)** (independent of amplitude)

prompt:
**(a)** Calculate the length of a simple pendulum with period 2.0 s on Earth. Take $g=9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$. **[2]**

**(b)** Calculate its period on the Moon, where $g=1.6\ \text{m s}^{-2}$. **[1]**

**(c)** Explain how a graph of $T^{2}$ against $l$ can be used to determine $g$. **[1]**
markscheme:
**(a)** $l=\dfrac{gT^{2}}{4\pi^{2}}=\dfrac{9.8\times4.0}{4\pi^{2}}=0.99$ m **(M1)(A1)**

**(b)** $T=2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{0.99}{1.6}}=4.9$ s **(A1)**

**(c)** $T^{2}=\dfrac{4\pi^{2}}{g}l$: a straight line through the origin with gradient $\dfrac{4\pi^{2}}{g}$, so $g=\dfrac{4\pi^{2}}{\text{gradient}}$ **(R1)** (valid for small angles)

prompt: For an undamped mass–spring oscillator, at which position is the kinetic energy maximum and the potential energy minimum?
options: Halfway between equilibrium and maximum displacement
markscheme: **A.** At equilibrium the speed is greatest and the displacement is zero; at the extremes all the energy is potential. The total energy stays constant without damping.

prompt: Two identical oscillators have displacements $x_1=x_0\sin\omega t$ and $x_2=x_0\sin\left(\omega t+\dfrac\pi2\right)$. State their phase difference and describe the position of oscillator 2 when oscillator 1 passes through equilibrium.
markscheme: Phase difference $\dfrac\pi2$ (a quarter cycle) **(A1)**; when $x_1=0$, oscillator 2 is at maximum displacement, momentarily at rest **(A1)**

prompt:
A 0.20 kg mass oscillates in SHM with amplitude 0.050 m and frequency 2.0 Hz, starting from the equilibrium position at $t=0$.

**(a)** Calculate the maximum speed and the total energy. **[3]**

**(b)** Calculate the speed when the displacement is 0.030 m. **[1]**

**(c)** Calculate the time taken to first reach a displacement of 0.025 m. **[2]**
markscheme:
**(a)** $\omega=4\pi=12.6\ \text{rad s}^{-1}$ **(A1)**; $v_{max}=\omega x_0=0.63\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ **(A1)**; $E_T=\tfrac12m\omega^{2}x_0^{2}=0.039$ J **(A1)**

**(b)** $v=\omega\sqrt{x_0^{2}-x^{2}}=12.6\times0.040=0.50\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ **(A1)**

**(c)** $x=x_0\sin\omega t$: $\sin\omega t=0.5\Rightarrow\omega t=\dfrac\pi6$ **(M1)**, $t=0.042$ s **(A1)** — this is $\tfrac{T}{12}$, only a third of the quarter-period, because the mass moves fastest near equilibrium.
